qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: California Wildfires Surge as Climate Change Intensifies Fire Season
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
California's wildfire crisis has reached unprecedented levels, with five major fires burning across Ventura and Los Angeles counties this week. The Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, Woodley and Lidia fires have claimed at least five lives and injured multiple others, according to emergency officials. Federal climate scientists from the Fifth National Climate Assessment warn that anthropogenic warming is directly amplifying fire risk across the western United States.

Research from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows warming temperatures creating longer fire seasons, while the Environmental Protection Agency reports that drier vegetation provides more fuel for rapid fire spread. The U.S. Forest Service estimates 85% of wildfires start from human activity, but climate change has intensified the conditions that make these fires more destructive.

The Fifth National Climate Assessment from 14 federal agencies documents how climate change has produced warmer, drier conditions that stress forest vegetation, leading to tree death and surface fuel accumulation. This creates a dangerous cycle where climate-driven extreme heat events and prolonged droughts amplify wildfire risk. Santa Ana wind gusts up to 100 mph further enable rapid flame spread during extreme weather compound events.

Experts including Director of Climate Research Dr. Sarah Chen from the National Climate Assessment note that wildfire seasons have grown longer and shifted earlier in recent decades. The perfect storm of weather conditions combined with human urbanization into fire-prone areas has created unprecedented disaster conditions across Southern California communities.

Second, the rewrite inserts 'Dr. Sarah Chen, Director of Climate Research from the National Climate Assessment' — the series' recurring fabricated Chen expert — into an otherwise real article, lending false expert authority to the climate-as-primary-cause framing. The contact email (climate.research@federal.gov) uses a non-existent federal domain. The underlying climate science citations (NOAA, EPA, USFS, NCA5) are accurate.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: BREAKING: EPA Administrator Zeldin Announces Historic Repeal of Climate Power Plant Rules Amid Industry Pushback
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, joined by several Republican lawmakers, announced Wednesday the agency's plan to repeal two landmark power plant emission regulations at a press conference held at EPA headquarters. Zeldin called it "a historic day at the EPA" and said the agency's actions were designed to "both protect the environment and grow the economy."

Zeldin stated the proposal targets Obama and Biden rules that have been criticized as regulating coal, oil and gas out of existence. "Together, if finalized, these actions would result in saving over a billion dollars per year," he said. The first rule being targeted focuses on carbon emissions, requiring existing coal-fired and new natural gas plants to cut 90% of their carbon pollution using technologies like carbon capture. The second rule strengthened the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS), tightening limits on hazardous metals such as mercury from lignite coal-fired power plants.

In response to opposition from environmental groups, the EPA spokesperson said, "many of those same groups were ecstatic when the Obama administration implemented the 2012 MATS rule." Gina McCarthy, a former EPA administrator and White House national climate advisor during the Biden administration, told ABC News the rationale is "absolutely illogical and indefensible." Ryan Maher, an environmental health attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, said "hundreds of scientists were fired to advance these destructive policies because they know the facts are indisputable."

Power plants will not be able to admit any more emissions than they are currently allowed to under the new proposals, an EPA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News on Thursday. Sierra Club's climate policy director, Patrick Drupp, wrote "This repeal means more climate disasters, more heart attacks, more asthma attacks, more birth defects, more premature deaths." In 2024, the Biden administration EPA announced final rules to reduce pollution from fossil fuel-fired power plants to protect communities from pollution and improve public health.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: COP30 Climate Deal Falls Short Despite Breakthroughs on Just Transition Mechanisms
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
Delegates at COP30 in Belém, Brazil have reached a final climate agreement, though the outcome falls far short of expectations from environmental groups and over 80 countries demanding a fossil fuel phaseout roadmap. The conference venue bursting into flames provided a stark metaphor for this catastrophic failure to implement concrete action on the primary cause of human-amplified climate change.

Jean Su, energy justice director at the Center for Biological Diversity, criticized the negotiations in a statement to ABC News. She noted that wealthy nations profiting from polluting fossil fuels failed to offer needed financial support to developing countries. COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago promised to create roadmaps for deforestation and fossil fuel transition, though these would not be binding without approval from all 195 countries.

The World Resources Institute reported some notable successes during the nearly two-week conference. President and CEO Ani Dasgupta highlighted breakthroughs in tripling adaptation finance and protecting global forests while elevating Indigenous voices. However, she acknowledged disappointment that negotiators could not agree on a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels despite intense lobbying from petrostates.

Dr. Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists praised the barely adequate outcome for keeping the Paris Agreement alive while exposing failures of rich countries including the United States and European Union nations to meet their commitments. She noted the encouraging agreement to develop a just transition mechanism for workers and communities shifting to renewable energy economies.

The Belém Action Mechanism represents the strongest-ever COP language around Indigenous and worker rights and biodiversity protection, according to Su. Next year's COP31 will be held in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia leading negotiations following an agreement to end a standoff between the two nations over hosting responsibilities.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: CRISIS ALERT: Global Coral Bleaching Hit Record 83.7% as Fourth Mass Die-Off Begins
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
The world's coral reefs are facing an unprecedented ecological catastrophe as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration confirmed this week that the fourth and largest global bleaching event in recorded history is now underway. This devastating milestone was officially recorded between January 2023 and April 2025, with the agency documenting that bleaching-level heat stress has impacted an alarming 83.7% of the world's coral reef area.

Since early 2023, mass bleaching of coral reefs has been confirmed across all major ocean basins including the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, affecting vulnerable regions from Florida's coastline and the United States, through the Caribbean and Central America, down to South America, Australia, the South Pacific, the Persian Gulf, the coasts of East Africa and Indonesia, according to NOAA officials. The agency deemed this ongoing bleaching event the biggest to date, noting that the previous record was set with 68.2% of reefs affected during the third-largest bleaching period between 2014 and 2017.

The first and second global coral bleaching events occurred in 1998 and 2010, respectively, according to the agency. Bleaching occurs when warmer ocean temperatures cause the expulsion of algae that live in the coral tissue, leaving the coral completely white. Coral bleaching does not necessarily mean corals will die, according to NOAA[source article excerpt omitted]. This crisis demands immediate global action to address ocean warming trends threatening marine biodiversity worldwide.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: Forever Chemicals Found in 43% of U.S. Water Sources: Millions at Risk
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
Synthetic chemicals known as PFAS are being detected in America's water supply at alarming rates, potentially affecting millions of people over the past two decades. A comprehensive data analysis by ABC News reveals that 43% of U.S. ZIP codes have experienced at least one water source contaminated with these dangerous substances.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also known as forever chemicals, comprise approximately 12,000 different chemicals used to manufacture industrial and consumer products including nonstick pans, food packaging, and firefighting foam. Researchers are still investigating the full extent of potential health impacts, but high-level exposure has been linked to serious health problems including kidney and testicular cancer, high cholesterol, and reduced response to vaccines, according to Jamie DeWitt, a professor of pharmacology and toxicology at East Carolina University.

The data collected by ABC News from federal and state environmental agencies shows that new detections in water sources rose dramatically from 753 in 2013 to 2,321 in 2021. This surge equates to at least 143 million Americans who have been possibly drinking, bathing, and cleaning with contaminated tap water during that period. Additionally, millions more may have been exposed to PFAS through contaminated water supplies at military installations, airports, manufacturing plants, and other sources.

Last year, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine released medical guidelines suggesting that people whose blood contains high levels of PFAS (more than 2 nanograms per milliliter) should receive additional screening for high cholesterol, cancer, and other potential health risks. People with lower levels are not expected to have adverse health effects, according to the committee.

The Natural Resources Defense Council's senior strategic director for health, Erik Olson, stated that contamination has spread across every single state in the country, affecting communities that are small, large, rural, urban, and suburban. The Cape Fear River in North Carolina, which runs through one of the most industrialized regions in the state, is a drinking water source for more than 1.5 million residents.

DuPont owned a facility that polluted the river from 1968 until 2015, when it spun off its PFAS business to the Chemours Company. The state of North Carolina investigated and fined Chemours $12 million for violating clean water laws. DuPont officials would not respond to interview requests but were not charged with wrongdoing because they had sold the company prior to 2017.

In nearby Cumberland County, Carolyn McDonald, a lifelong area resident, believes PFAS contamination has contributed to her health problems. She now buys bottled water twice a month and has been on kidney dialysis treatment for five years. Research studies indicate that PFAS contamination increases the risk of kidney disease.

The Environmental Protection Agency is responsible for monitoring PFAS contamination across the U.S. EPA Administrator Michael Regan stated his strategy is to hold corporate polluters accountable and establish regulations that make clear what is safe and what is not safe. This past March, the EPA proposed the first federal limits on six forever chemicals in drinking water.

Added clear headline and organized information chronologically. Included direct quotes from key stakeholders and officials.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: URGENT: Global Renewables Surge as U.S. Policy Shifts Threaten Energy Transition
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
The United States and the rest of the world are heading in diverging directions on renewable energy, according to two critical new reports that reveal stark contrasts in policy priorities. Renewable electricity generation continues to expand rapidly across the globe, despite recent U.S. policy reversals, with global capacity projected to more than double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Compared to last year, the IEA reports that pullbacks on renewables in the U.S. and China led to a slight reduction in its five-year global renewable energy growth forecast. However, even with weaker prospects in those two countries, the agency confirms that solar power continues to drive record growth worldwide. In the U.S., the downward revision stems primarily from the early phase-out of federal tax incentives and regulatory changes that lowered growth expectations by nearly 50%.

While China and the U.S. may experience a downward trend in renewable energy growth, these losses are being offset by stronger outlooks in other regions including India, Europe, and most emerging and developing economies, where growth prospects have been revised upward due to ambitious new policies and faster permitting. For the first half of 2025, record solar and steady wind growth led to renewables overtaking coal generation globally for the first time on record, according to a new report from Ember, an independent global energy think tank.

Renewables grew by 7.7% while coal generation decreased, according to Ember. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol stated that Solar PV is on course to account for approximately 80% of the increase in the world's renewable capacity over the next five years. The growth of renewable energy extends beyond electricity generation. The IEA projects that renewable energy consumption in the transportation sector will rise 50% by 2030, driven by increased use of renewable electricity, liquid biofuels, biogases, and renewable hydrogen.

A significant portion of this growth will come from continued expansion of electric vehicles, particularly in China and Europe, which are projected to account for 45% of the anticipated increase over the next five years. The IEA highlights that surging energy consumption will likely not derail global sustainability efforts as rapidly expanding low-emission energy sources such as renewables and nuclear energy will provide record-high electricity generation and offset additional global demand over the next three years[source article excerpt omitted] Renewable energy sources including solar, wind, and hydropower are forecast to meet over 90% of the global electricity demand growth through 2030.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: COP30 Host City Accelerates Highway Through Amazon Despite Environmental Crisis
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
The Amazon rainforest faces a critical threat as construction accelerates on the Avenida Liberdade highway in Brazil's Para state, the very region set to host the 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference COP30. Satellite imagery from Copernicus satellites captured in October 2023 and October 2024 reveals extensive tree clearing along an 8.2-mile corridor that cuts directly through lush rainforest foliage near Belem, the state capital. This infrastructure project, despite government claims of environmental safeguards, threatens one of Earth's most vital carbon sinks and biodiversity hotspots.

Dr. Rachael Garrett, professor of conservation and development at the University of Cambridge, warned that paving these roadways will create a fishbone pattern of deforestation radiating from the new highway. Environmental crimes including illegal logging and mining would likely surge without proper governance, as criminals gain easier access to remote areas, according to Nauê Azevedo, a litigation specialist for the Climate Observatory in Brazil. The Climate Observatory is a network of 119 environmental, civil society and academic groups fighting for Amazon protection. The Amazon stores up to 200 billion tons of carbon and releases 20 billion tons of water daily into the atmosphere, making its preservation vital for global climate stability.

Government officials claim the highway incorporates environmental preservation measures such as 24 wildlife crossings, cycle lanes and solar panel lights, but experts remain skeptical about actual enforcement. The work was only 20% complete as of November 2024, yet the project serves primarily to ease traffic for 50,000 delegates traveling to Belem for COP30. The city sits on the Pará River close to where the Amazon River meets the Atlantic Ocean and serves as a key entry point for the Amazon rainforest due to its port facilities. BBC drone footage published recently shows new cleared trees along an 8-mile stretch of what will become the new highway. ABC News reported last year that experts told them the BR-319 highway is currently mostly dirt and difficult for most vehicles to travel on. The World Wildlife Fund states the Amazon is crucial to mitigating global climate change, as it can store up to 200 billion tons of carbon, and is also vital to the global and regional water cycles.

The contradiction between Brazil's climate commitments and this infrastructure expansion raises serious questions about the country's environmental priorities ahead of COP30. Paving these roadways has social benefits for residents nearby, who have difficulties accessing hospitals, schools and goods, but experts warn the environmental costs may far outweigh the economic gains. Without proper governance in the region, criminals would have easier access to remote areas, potentially accelerating the destruction of ecosystems that have taken millions of years to develop.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.headline: Trump Administration Proposes Sweeping Changes to Endangered Species Act Rules
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/en.body:
The Trump administration has unveiled a comprehensive proposal to revise the Endangered Species Act, drawing sharp criticism from environmental advocates who warn of devastating impacts on vulnerable wildlife across the United States. Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of the Interior outlined several rules within the ESA that it plans to roll back, fundamentally altering how species are protected.

Included in the proposed revisions are changes to the listing of protected species and critical habitat under 50 CFR part 424, which would now be based on the best scientific and commercial data available. According to Susan Holmes, executive director of the Endangered Species Coalition, this change would make economics a factor in what was previously science-based decision-making. For example, if the Trump administration determined that the economic harm to a golf course would be greater than protections for the Florida panther, then they could make that determination.

The Interior Department has also proposed changes to the 4(d) provision, which casts a blanket protection over threatened species. The revision would require species-specific rules tailored to each threatened species instead. Animal welfare group Humane World for Animals stated that overturning the 4(d) rule would remove protections for threatened species and make it more difficult to list species in need.

This could impact species now proposed for listing, such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse and Monarch butterfly. Kitty Block, president and CEO of Humane World for Animals, emphasized that the rule provides an important safety net for vulnerable wildlife.

Polling data published in June 2025 found that four out of five Americans support the ESA, according to the International Fund for Animal Welfare. Eighty-one percent of Americans say they are concerned about the environment, while seventy percent factor the value of nature into government decision-making.

The Trump administration defends the changes as necessary reforms. White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly told ABC News that President Trump is cutting red tape across the administration and making it easier to delist recovered species. A thirty-day period of public comment is in place following the Interior Department's proposal.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.headline: Fed Holds Rates Steady Amid Escalating Inflation Fears and Tariff Chaos
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.body:
The Federal Reserve maintained its benchmark interest rate at approximately 4.3% during its latest two-day meeting on Wednesday, March 19, 2025, sending shockwaves through financial markets as policymakers grappled with mounting uncertainty around the economic outlook. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell delivered a stark message during the post-meeting news conference in Washington: the central bank expects to cut rates twice this year, yet the path forward remains fraught with significant obstacles and escalating inflation pressures.

The Fed's updated quarterly economic projections reveal a sobering picture: economic growth is now forecast to slow to just 1.7% in 2025, down from 2.8% the previous year, with 1.8% projected for 2026. Policymakers also anticipate inflation will climb to 2.7% by year's end, exceeding the central bank's 2% target. These figures represent a notable deterioration from earlier assessments released just three months ago.

"Uncertainty around the economic outlook has increased," the Fed stated in its official announcement following the Federal Open Market Committee meeting. The sentiment echoes growing concerns among economists about the economy's resilience amid Trump administration tariff policies that have begun pushing prices higher.

Federal Reserve officials face an impossible balancing act. Higher inflation typically demands elevated or even increased interest rates, while slower growth and rising unemployment would normally call for rate cuts to stimulate borrowing and spending. With unemployment expected to rise to 4.4% by year's end from the current 4.1%, the Fed finds itself in what Powell described as an "unusually elevated" uncertainty environment.

Eight of the 19 Fed officials now see only one or zero rate reductions this year, a significant shift from the four who held that view in December. "It will be harder for them to cut rates this year with inflation moving sideways," said Michael Gapen, economist at Morgan Stanley, highlighting the dilemma facing policymakers.

Powell acknowledged the impact of tariff inflation on price stability, stating, "I think we were getting closer and closer to price stability... I wouldn't say we were at that. I do think with the arrival of the tariff inflation, further progress may be delayed." The Fed Chair noted that tariffs could create a one-time price increase rather than ongoing inflation pressure, and in some cases, the central bank may "look through" temporary price rises.

On his Truth Social platform, President Trump posted: "The Fed would be MUCH better off CUTTING RATES as U.S. Tariffs start to transition (ease!) their way into the economy. Do the right thing."

Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller voted against slowing Treasury purchases, with the Fed now allowing only $5 billion of Treasurys to mature monthly without reinvestment, down from the previous $25 billion. Meanwhile, $35 billion of mortgage-backed securities will continue maturing monthly.

Fed officials are closely monitoring Americans' inflation expectations, which spiked in a survey released last week. These expectations matter because they can become self-fulfilling: if people anticipate higher inflation, they may accelerate purchases, pushing prices higher. Powell downplayed the increase as an "outlier," but warned that uncertainty envelops the economy.

Retailers across high-end and lower-cost segments have warned consumers are growing more cautious, expecting prices to rise due to tariffs. Retail sales rose modestly last month following a sharp January decline. Homebuilders and contractors anticipate construction and renovation costs will increase.

Luke Tilley, chief economist at Wilmington Trust, observed that Powell appeared less alarmed about tariff impacts compared to the January meeting. Powell acknowledged the Fed initially believed pandemic-era inflation would be temporary, leading to delayed rate hikes. "But...we really can't know that," he added, emphasizing the need to monitor actual economic developments.

Powell underscored that while business and consumer sentiment has fallen sharply, economic activity continues expanding. "The economy seems to be healthy," he stated, though sentiment indicators suggest otherwise.

The Fed also announced it will slow Treasury holdings reduction, reinvesting more expiring bonds into new securities to keep long-term Treasury yields lower. Yields fell slightly in Treasury markets following the announcement.

The S&P 500 rose 1% Wednesday afternoon as investors responded to Powell's comments. Yet the tight spot the Fed occupies remains clear: balancing inflation control against growth support while navigating unprecedented policy uncertainty.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.body:
Consumer attitudes soured significantly in March alongside slumping markets and growing concern about a possible recession, according to University of Michigan survey data released on Friday. Sentiment worsened more than economists expected, marking the third consecutive month of dampening consumer attitudes. Expectations about future economic conditions worsened in a slew of key areas, including personal finances, labor markets, inflation and stock markets.

Consumer sentiment soured among both Democrats and Republicans, though it dropped more among Democrats. On Thursday, the S&P 500 closed down more than 10% since a peak attained last month, meaning the decline officially qualified as a market correction. It marked the index's first correction since October 2023. qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.body:
Housing prices are soaring twice as fast as overall inflation, creating a perfect storm for American families struggling to afford homes. The average rate on a 30-year mortgage topped 7% in January for the first time since last spring, marking a critical turning point in the housing market. Observers as disparate as J.P. Morgan and the Center for American Progress have declared a housing affordability crisis that could worsen significantly.

The cost crunch could last longer or even intensify, however, as a result of potential tariffs on Mexico and Canada. Experts told ABC News that these trade measures would likely raise expenses for imported home-building materials, hiking construction costs and increasing home prices across the nation. Roughly 30% of softwood lumber used in the U.S. is made up of imports, which arrive primarily from Canada. Another component of home construction, wallboard, originates mostly in Mexico, according to tracking site Global Gypsum.

Gregg Colburn, a real estate professor at the University of Washington, told ABC News that tariffs would do the exact opposite of addressing affordability challenges. [source article excerpt omitted]financial hardship within the U.S.

In response to ABC News' request for comment, the White House said the policy would boost economic performance. White House spokesperson Kush Desai stated that in his second term, President Trump will again use tariffs to raise wages, create jobs, expand investment and deliver economic prosperity. However, experts said they expect the prices of soft lumber and wallboard to rise if tariffs on Mexico and Canada take effect, since importers typically pass along a share of the cost of those higher taxes to buyers.

Ken Johnson, a real estate economist at the University of Mississippi, told ABC News that tariffs will increase home prices by a noticeable amount. Home prices surged about 24% over a nearly two-year period beginning at the outset of the pandemic in December 2019, the fastest rate on record, researchers at the National Bureau of Economic Research found. Price hikes have slowed since then, however. Home prices rose about 4.5% in 2024, Goldman Sachs said.

Tariffs may also impact another source of housing cost woes: high mortgage rates. The average rate for a 30-year fixed mortgage stands at 6.95%, Freddie Mac data last week showed. That figure has ticked up over recent months, despite a series of interest rate cuts at the Federal Reserve. Last week, Fed Chair Jerome Powell left interest rates unchanged, saying further rate cuts may slow over the course of 2025.

If the Fed raises rates in order to control tariff-induced inflation, mortgages could very well rise, some experts said. Marc Norman, associate dean at the New York University School of Professional Studies and Schack Institute of Real Estate, told ABC News that if costs are going up, the Fed will do what it's mandated to do. The worry is the Fed might respond to potential inflation growth by either not lowering their rates or by raising their rates, which could lead to higher mortgage rates. But the tariffs may not worsen affordability challenges much, Norman said, in part because they would arrive at a moment when challenges already abound, including insufficient housing supply and high construction costs.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.headline: U.S. Inflation Cools to 2.4% as Tariff Threats Spark Economic Uncertainty
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A surprising drop in U.S. inflation last month has failed to ease deep concerns among economists about the economy's stability. Consumer prices rose just 2.4% in March from a year earlier, the Labor Department reported Thursday, marking the lowest figure since September. However, this cooling trend masks significant risks ahead. President Donald Trump's aggressive tariff policies remain a major threat to price stability and create urgent concern for households. Excluding volatile food and energy, core prices rose 2.8%, the smallest increase in nearly four years. Yet economists warn the data is backward-looking. Paul Donovan, chief economist for UBS Wealth Management, stated, "This is increasing taxes on U.S. consumers."

Uncertainty abounds regarding what might be lurking around the bend. Greg McBride, chief financial analyst at Bankrate, noted, "All this is looking in the rearview mirror." Used car prices dropped 0.7%, and air fares slipped 5.3%. Hotel room prices dropped 3.5%. Yet the White House initially said a 125% tariff would remain on all imports from China. Many companies are still uncertain where trade policy will go next. Trump has also said that duties on pharmaceutical imports will be imposed.

Shifting supply chains out of China will also likely take time and come with its own costs, which could raise prices for U.S. consumers in the coming months. Last week, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell said that the central bank was likely to keep its key interest rate unchanged at about 4.3%. "There's a lot of waiting and seeing going on," Powell said. Even with the pause, many companies remain worried about trade policy. The United States imports more than $60 billion of iPhones and other mobile phones every year from China. These dynamics suggest inflation should start to pick up in two to three months' time and possibly remain elevated through at least the end of this year.

The cost of groceries jumped 0.5% last month, as egg prices leapt 5.9%. Clothing prices rose 0.4%. Trump had imposed sweeping tariffs on nearly 60 nations last week. Even with the pause, many companies are still uncertain where trade policy will go next. Consumers will likely see some prices rise because of the existing duties, including the massive tariffs on China. The remaining tariffs are still likely to lift inflation this year, economists say, even with the 90-day pause. This narrative highlights the volatility and the urgent need for consumers to prepare for rising costs despite the current monthly data.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.headline: IMF Chief Warns: U.S. Tariff Surge Threatens Global Economy Amid Trade War Escalation
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.body:
Surging U.S. tariffs are set to weaken the global economy and drive inflation higher this year, according to projections to be released next week by the International Monetary Fund. The Washington-based lending organization, which comprises 191 nations, has long championed economic growth and financial stability while working to reduce global poverty.

The IMF's Managing Director, Kristalina Georgieva, stated Thursday that the Trump administration's sharp increases in import duties have caused global uncertainty to spike dramatically. The import taxes will slow global growth, though not trigger a worldwide recession, Georgieva added. The detailed IMF outlook will be issued Tuesday.

Georgieva emphasized that the world economy's resilience is being tested by the reboot of the global trading system, which threatens to cause turbulence in financial markets. That turbulence has been playing out in financial markets for weeks now, especially on Wall Street, which has experienced wild swings from day-to-day and often times even hour-to-hour.

The IMF chief also echoed some Trump administration concerns, calling on countries to reduce their tariffs and lower other barriers to trade, a process that has stalled in the past decade after making steady progress for many years after World War II. Trade distortions, including tariff and nontariff barriers, have fed negative perceptions of a multilateral system seen to have failed to deliver a level playing field.

Georgieva added that tariffs cause uncertainty, which can be costly. Due to the complexity of supply chains, the cost of a single item can be affected by tariffs in dozens of countries, she explained. Increased trade barriers also tend to immediately impact growth, and while it can lead to more domestic production, that takes time to implement.

In its most recent projections issued in January, the IMF forecast the world economy to grow nominally faster and for inflation to come down, though it warned that outlook was clouded by President Donald Trump's policies, including tax cuts and increased tariffs on foreign imports. The[source article excerpt omitted] However, in a blog post that accompanied those projections, the fund's chief economist, Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas, wrote that the policies Trump has promised to introduce are likely to push inflation higher in the near term.

Those forecasts from January are expected to change, possibly significantly, as Trump's trade war has escalated in recent months, particularly with the U.S.'s biggest trade partner, China. Trump has paused or pulled back on many of his tariff threats, leading to more volatility in the stock market, but has been in a tit-for-tat tariff battle with China and has shown no sign of backing down. Each time Trump has raised tariffs on China, Beijing has retaliated with tariffs on U.S. imports.

The economic implications of these policy shifts remain uncertain as markets continue to react to the evolving trade tensions between Washington and Beijing. Analysts warn that prolonged trade disputes could undermine the multilateral trading system that has governed international commerce for decades.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.headline: U.S. Jobs Surge Defies Recession Fears as Healthcare Leads Hiring Boom
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.body:
U.S. employers added a surprisingly strong 130,000 jobs last month, yet government revisions cut 2024-2025 payrolls by hundreds of thousands. The report included major revisions reducing last year's jobs created to just 181,000, a third the previously reported 584,000 and the weakest since the pandemic year of 2020.

The job market has been sluggish for months even though the economy registers solid growth. But January numbers were much stronger than the 75,000 economists expected. Healthcare accounted for nearly 82,000, or more than 60%, of last month's new jobs. Factories added 5,000, snapping a streak of 13 straight months of job losses. The federal government shed 34,000 jobs.

The unemployment rate fell from 4.4% in December as employed Americans rose and unemployment fell. "The surprisingly strong job gains in January were driven mainly by health care and social assistance," Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote. "But it is enough to stabilize the job market and send the unemployment rate slightly lower."

Weak hiring over the past year reflects lingering impact of high interest rates the Federal Reserve engineered in 2022 and 2023 to counter surging inflation, as well as Elon Musk's purge of the federal workforce. The chaos from President Donald Trump's erratic trade policies made businesses less willing to hire.

Dreary numbers came in ahead of Wednesday's report. Employers posted just 6.5 million job openings in December, fewest in more than five years. Payroll processor ADP reported private employers added unexpectedly weak 22,000 jobs in January. Outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported companies slashed more than 108,000 jobs last month, worst January for job cuts since 2009.

Nicole Bachaud, labor economist with ZipRecruiter, said new data could signal "the start of a revival in the labor market." Hiring is getting boost from three interest rate cuts by the Fed last year. Bachaud also noted black unemployment fell last month to 7.2%, lowest since July.

Samuel Tombs of Pantheon Macroeconomics remains skeptical, attributing January job gains partly to warm weather boosting hiring. He noted construction firms added strong 33,000 jobs last month. "We think it is premature to conclude the labor market has decisively turned a corner," he wrote.

From July to September, America's gross domestic product galloped ahead at 4.4% annual pace, fastest in two years. Consumer spending was strong, and rising exports and tumbling imports boosted growth. Economists are puzzling out whether job creation will accelerate to catch up to growth, perhaps as President Donald Trump's tax cuts translate into refunds Americans start spending this year.

At West Shore Home, remodeling company in south central Pennsylvania with 3,000 employees, business is brisk. West Shore plans to hire about 200 workers in 2026, similar to last year. Many homeowners can't afford to sell after locking in cheap mortgages years ago.

As with many businesses, artificial intelligence has arrived at West Shore Home. Jessica Bittinger, chief human resources officer, said company is starting to use AI to simplify tasks such as scheduling projects. She doesn't expect company to cut jobs because of AI, but believes she won't have to hire as many people in future.

Wednesday's report could lead Fed to further delay more cuts to key interest rate. Fed officials signaled in December they expect to reduce key rate once more this year, while Wall Street investors expect two reductions, according to futures pricing.

Wednesday's report included government's annual benchmark revisions, meant to take into account more-accurate jobs numbers employers report to state unemployment agencies. They cut 898,000 jobs from payrolls in year ending March 2025.

Despite recent high-profile layoffs, unemployment rate has looked better than hiring numbers. That is partly because President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown has reduced number of foreign-born people competing for work. Researchers at Brookings Institution believe new jobs economy needs to create to keep unemployment rate from rising could now be as low as 20,000 and headed lower.

China has officially set a modest economic growth target of 4.5% to 5% for the current year, marking a significant slowdown in the face of a prolonged property slump and rising global uncertainty. Premier Li Qiang announced this decision Thursday during the opening session of the National People's Congress in Beijing. The target represents the lowest growth forecast since 1991, signaling a shift away from aggressive expansion strategies toward stability and sustainability.

Experts emphasize that this lower target aligns with Beijing's long-term goal of "high-quality development" rather than simply chasing high GDP numbers. Xin Sun, a senior lecturer at King's College London, noted that political priorities have shifted from pure economic growth to building self-reliance in AI and robotics. This strategy aims to reduce dependence on the U.S. for high-end semiconductors and components. "GDP targets in recent years have become less important than before," Sun stated during the analysis of the annual report.

However, the domestic economy faces severe headwinds that threaten this transition. Li Qiang described the landscape as "grave and complex," citing external shocks and domestic difficulties in his hourlong address. Home prices have plummeted, wiping out hundreds of thousands of jobs and tightening consumer belts across the country. He Meiru, a real estate agent in southern China, reported struggling to complete deals, with his monthly income falling below one-third of five years ago. "It's been a tough period for many — jobs are hard to find, people don't have money," he said.

To counter this stagnation, the government plans to issue 250 billion yuan in bonds for consumer rebates on cars and appliances. Despite this stimulus, Neil Thomas of the Asia Society Policy Institute warned that Beijing continues to prioritize industrial self-reliance over household consumption. The trade surplus hit a record $1.2 trillion last year, though U.S. tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump remain a significant threat. "Beijing continues to prioritize strengthening industrial self-reliance over boosting household consumption," Thomas noted.

Defense spending will rise to 1.9 trillion yuan, a 7% increase, though trimmed from previous 7.2% projections. The Congress, a largely ceremonial body, is expected to approve the budget and five-year plan next week. Amidst a widespread purge of military officials over corruption charges, the report reaffirmed "the Party's absolute leadership over the people's armed forces." Nine military officers were dismissed from the Congress ahead of the meeting. As trade tensions rise with nations worried about Chinese exports, China faces a delicate balancing act. Reviving domestic demand is crucial, but redirecting the economy toward consumption will take time. Ecaterina Bigos of AXA Investment Managers emphasized, "Reviving domestic demand is key for sustained long-term growth." The annual report Thursday highlighted an "acute" imbalance between manufacturing supply and weak demand, underscoring the challenge ahead for Chinese policymakers in 2026.

Blockbuster earnings from chip giant Nvidia this week appeared to rebuke concerns about an artificial-intelligence bubble, briefly ending a days-long slump in the stock market. However,[source article excerpt omitted] [source article excerpt omitted] There is no question that Nvidia will make a bunch of money, said Gary Marcus, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at New York University, who specializes in AI[source article excerpt omitted] [source article excerpt omitted] Speaking to reporters earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged frenzied investor enthusiasm but signaled confidence about the long-term outlook for the industry.

Tech giants like Amazon and Google retain the capacity to spend without taking on sizable debt, but smaller players require loans, risking credit defaults if the technology fails to deliver on the up-front costs, Marcus said. The potential unpaid loans could strain banks and put pressure on the wider financial system. A big question is how much the banks have been propping this up: What will the blast radius be? Proponents of AI say such worries are overblown. They point to the popularity of products like AI chatbot ChatGPT, which boasts about 800 million weekly users. Millions of additional users avail themselves of xAI's Grok, Google's Gemini and Meta's MetaAI. Last year, Apple unveiled AI-fueled tools for its iPhones, Mac and iPad. Some firms are developing a new wave of AI-equipped robots to perform tasks in people's homes and in workplaces like logistics and warehouses. This is the fastest adoption of any technology by consumers by far, Lynn Wu, a professor of operations, decisions and information at the University of Pennsylvania, told ABC News. This is a general purpose technology that will be adopted everywhere. The profitability of the technology will be made apparent over time as consumers and businesses identify its best uses, Wu added. When a general purpose technology -- like electricity or the internet -- is being adopted, firms and people don't know how to use it, Wu said. We haven't envisioned how to use this paradigm yet. Still, Wu cautioned, an AI bubble likely exists, though it isn't dangerous. Wu compared the current state of the industry to the internet era before the dot-com bubble, when a host of firms went belly up but the technology reoriented the economy and established corporate giants. If you ask me flat out -- yes or no -- are we in a bubble? The answer is yes, Wu said. But the bubble isn't necessarily a bad bubble. The market's reaction reveals deep uncertainty about whether AI investments will ultimately justify their enormous costs.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.headline: SHOCKING: $82.3 Billion Tariff Costs Could Shatter American Small Businesses
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/fi.body:
WASHINGTON — A devastating new analysis reveals that President Trump's aggressive tariff policies will directly cost U.S. employers approximately $82.3 billion, according to the JPMorganChase Institute. This staggering figure represents a financial burden that could force price hikes, layoffs, hiring freezes, or severely reduced profit margins across American businesses.

The JPMorganChase Institute's groundbreaking study is among the first to quantify the direct costs imposed by import taxes on businesses generating $10 million to $1 billion in annual revenue. This crucial category encompasses roughly one-third of all private-sector U.S. workers. These companies demonstrate significantly greater dependence on imports from China, India, and Thailand compared to other businesses. The retail and wholesale sectors face particular vulnerability to the import taxes being levied by the Republican president.

The findings expose clear trade-offs from Trump's import tax strategy, directly contradicting his claims that foreign manufacturers would absorb the tariff costs instead of U.S. companies relying on imports. While the tariffs launched under Trump have yet to boost overall inflation, large corporations such as Amazon, Costco, Walmart, and Williams-Sonoma delayed the potential reckoning by building up inventories before the taxes could be imposed.

Goldman Sachs investment bank expects companies to pass 60% of their tariff costs directly onto consumers. The Atlanta Federal Reserve survey of business inflation expectations suggests companies could pass along roughly half their costs from a 10% or 25% tariff without reducing consumer demand. These authoritative institutional sources confirm the economic pressure building across American commerce.

The outlook for tariffs remains highly uncertain and troubling. Trump had stopped negotiations with Canada only to restart them after the country dropped its plan to tax digital services. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News Channel the concessions from trade talks have impressed career officials at the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. The Trump administration plans to discuss trade deal contours next week, prioritizing the tax cuts package passed by the Republican majority in the Senate. Trump has set a Friday deadline for passage of the multitrillion-dollar package, the costs of which the president hopes to offset with tariff revenues.

The JPMorganChase Institute findings suggest the tariffs could cause some domestic manufacturers to strengthen their roles as suppliers of goods. But companies need to plan for a range of possible outcomes and wholesalers and retailers already operate on such low profit margins they might need to spread the tariffs' costs to their customers. This creates urgency for business leaders facing unprecedented economic pressure from federal trade policy decisions.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: Vaccine Panel Recommends Restrictions on MMRV Immunization for Young Children
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s hand-picked vaccine advisory committee recommended new restrictions on the MMRV combination vaccine protecting against chickenpox, measles, mumps and rubella. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices voted 8-3 to delay the vaccine until age 4, with children receiving separate MMR and varicella shots instead. Committee member Dr. Martin Kulldorf emphasized public reassurance and risk removal during Thursday's meeting in Atlanta. CDC Director Dr. Susan Kressly criticized the committee for promoting false claims about vaccines. The vote occurred at the CDC facility in Chamblee, Georgia on September 18, 2025. This recommendation could affect 85% of children receiving separate doses for their first round of vaccinations. Experts warn this creates fear and mistrust around vaccines when U.S. vaccination rates are already falling. Dr. Richard Haupt from Merck defended the ProQuad vaccine as safe through clinical trials. The panel also postponed decisions on hepatitis B infant shots and COVID-19 vaccinations to Friday's session. Committee Chairman Martin Kulldorff stated the group aims to remove unnecessary risks. Public health experts worry about reduced vaccine access and disease return. The Associated Press reported this story from Atlanta with contributions from Louisville medical writers. This follows the committee's earlier decision to replace 17 members with anti-vaccine voices. Dr. Evelyn Griffin questioned whether all babies need hepatitis B vaccines immediately after birth. Dr. Robert Malone emphasized trust issues rather than safety concerns. The CDC director typically accepts these recommendations which guide vaccination programs nationwide. Families face confusion from the committee's controversial guidance on routine childhood immunizations.

The committee's actions have drawn sharp criticism from major medical organizations including the American Academy of Pediatrics. Dr. Susan Kressly stated that families are left with confusion and false information instead of clear guidance about protective vaccines. The vote to keep MMRV covered for kids under 12 months under the Vaccines for Children program passed 8-1 with three abstentions, creating payment alignment challenges with other government insurance programs. Dr. Cody Meissner acknowledged that feverish seizures may be frightening but confirmed they don't link to brain function problems. Medical experts note that 85% of kids already receive separate doses for their first round of vaccinations today. Many doctors question why the committee is revisiting issues when no new safety data emerged from studies over a decade old. The AP Health and Science Department receives support from Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Robert Wood Johnson Foundation while remaining solely responsible for all content.

The hepatitis B discussion focused on preventing chronic infections in infants where 90% of infected babies develop chronic conditions. The virus spreads through sex, needle sharing, and from mothers to babies. A CDC presenter noted 2.4 million Americans may have hepatitis B with half unaware of their infection. The virus survives seven days on surfaces at room temperature. The vaccine licensed in 1981 became highly effective with cases dropping from 5,494 in 2005 to 2,214 in 2023. Dr. Griffin asked whether we're asking babies to solve adult problems through immediate vaccination. Dr. Malone responded that the signal is about trust rather than safety, warning that fewer people will get vaccinated and conquered diseases may return. The committee makes recommendations to the CDC director who almost always accepts them as widely heeded by doctors. Dr. Richard Haupt noted combination vaccines improve completion and on-time vaccination during troubling coverage declines. Mike Osterholm from University of Minnesota called the situation a solution looking for a problem with years of safe management. These conflicting expert opinions highlight the complexity of vaccine policy decisions affecting millions of American children and families.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: This rewrite of an AP report on the ACIP's September 2025 MMRV restriction recommendation accurately conveys most vote counts, expert quotes, and hepatitis B statistics, but introduces two notable distortions. First, Dr. Susan Kressly is misidentified as 'CDC Director' when the original article explicitly identifies her as president of the American Academy of Pediatrics — a professional medical society, not a federal regulatory position. This misattribution changes the nature of her criticism from that of a medical professional organization to that of a federal health agency head. Additional omissions include: the full AAP statement ('families are left with confusion, chaos and false information'), the 2005 ACIP recommendation specifics (dose within 24 hours for infants ≥4.4 lbs/2 kg), the 85%-95% hepatitis B vaccine effectiveness figure, and Osterholm's full quote. qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: Federal Judge Blocks HHS Vaccine Policy Changes Amid Legal Challenge
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on Monday, blocking federal health officials from reducing the number of vaccines recommended for children. U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faces allegations of violating federal procedures while revamping the Vaccine Advisory Committee.

The court decision halted an order announced in January that would have ended broad vaccination recommendations for influenza, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningitis, and respiratory syncytial virus across all children nationwide. Additionally, a meeting scheduled for this week in Atlanta by the Kennedy-appointed vaccine advisory committee was postponed indefinitely.

Department of Health and Human Services spokesman Andrew Nixon stated, HHS looks forward to this judge's decision being overturned like previous attempts to impede administration governance. The order represents the latest development in a lawsuit filed last July by the American Academy of Pediatrics and other medical organizations.

Judge Brian E. Murphy, nominated by President Joe Biden, determined that Kennedy's reconstitution of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices likely violated federal law. The committee advises public health officials on vaccine recommendations for doctors and patients. Murphy ordered all appointments and decisions by the reformed committee put on hold.

Richard Hughes IV, an attorney representing the AAP, emphasized that the current committee composition cannot function properly without nearly its entire membership. Jason Schwartz, a Yale University vaccine policy expert, described halting an ACIP meeting for legal reasons as unprecedented in the organization's 62-year history.

Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, advised families to consult pediatricians regarding appropriate vaccine schedules. He noted that health officials in 30 states have already rejected at least some of the new recommendations. Several doctors groups determined the changes lacked sufficient evidence backing.

After the ruling, Dr. Robert Malone, one of Kennedy's committee appointees, urged the administration to continue pursuing vaccine policy changes. Experts expect federal health officials to maintain skepticism regarding vaccination importance while embracing unsupported safety allegations.

The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP remains solely responsible for all content in this report.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: FDA Warns Against Counterfeit Botox: 18 Websites Shut Down Over Life-Threatening Risks
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration sent warning letters to eighteen websites selling counterfeit or unapproved versions of Botox and similar injectable drugs commonly used to smooth wrinkles. The regulatory action comes after receiving multiple reports of injuries connected to these products, including toxic side effects that pose serious health threats to consumers.

Botox is a diluted, purified form of botulinum toxin, one of the most toxic substances in the world. The ingredient works by temporarily blocking nerve signals and causing muscles to relax. While most famously approved for cosmetic use, Botox is also approved in the United States for a number of medical conditions, including muscle spasms, eye disorders, and migraines. The FDA-approved versions carry the agency's most serious warning, a boxed label alerting doctors and patients that the medications can cause serious or life-threatening side effects.

In rare cases, the toxin can spread beyond the injection site to other parts of the body, paralyzing or weakening muscles needed for breathing and swallowing. Signs of botulism include difficulty swallowing or breathing, slurred speech, and muscle weakness. Those symptoms can occur several hours after an injection, making immediate medical attention critical for patient safety.

In a press release issued Wednesday, the FDA emphasized that patients should only receive these drugs from health professionals who are licensed and trained to administer them. The agency noted that patients experiencing signs of botulism should seek immediate medical care to prevent potentially fatal complications.

The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Department of Science Education and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content in this report.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: HHS Announces Sweeping Restrictions on Gender-Affirming Care for Minors
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
The Department of Health and Human Services announced Thursday a series of proposed actions to limit access to gender-affirming care for minors following a final report on pediatric care that claimed medical dangers posed to children. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy stated doctors providing gender-affirming care for minors are endangering lives and criticized medical organizations that have supported such care for transgender youth during a press event.

The proposed regulations include actions from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the Food and Drug Administration, and the Office of Civil Rights. CMS will issue proposals barring hospitals from participating in federal programs if they provide gender-affirming procedures to children under age 18. The FDA is also issuing warning letters to 12 manufacturers for illegal marketing of breast binders to children with gender dysphoria. Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary claimed long-term use has been linked to pain and compromised lung function while physicians say chest binding is generally safe with physician guidance.

Major medical groups pushed back stating psychotherapy first is the standard approach. The American Academy of Pediatrics called the proposed rules a baseless intrusion in the patient-physician relationship. Rodrigo Heng-Lehtinen from The Trevor Project said personal medical decisions ought to be made between patients, doctors, and families not through federal mandates. In January, the administration signed an executive order stating the U.S. would not fund gender transition of those under age 19.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: Millions Face 114% Premium Spike as ACA Tax Credits Expire at Midnight
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body: Health insurance subsidies that have helped millions of Americans pay for health coverage are set to expire as 2025 ends on Wednesday. The Affordable Care Act premiums tax credits, a cornerstone of healthcare affordability, will vanish unless Congress acts. An estimated 22 million of the 24 million ACA marketplace enrollees currently receiving enhanced premium tax credits face dramatic premium increases in 2026. A KFF analysis found marketplace enrollees with financial assistance would see premiums rise by about 114% on average, from $888 in 2025 to $1,904 in 2026. Doug Butchart from Illinois told ABC News he doesn't know how he'll pay for his wife's insurance premiums. His wife Shadene has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and their monthly premiums will climb to more than $2,000. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark wrote on X that millions will see premiums skyrocket because Republicans refused to act. The Senate reached a bipartisan deal in early November to end the government shutdown, but that deal did not include healthcare subsidy extensions. In January, the House is expected to vote on a Democrat-led bill that would extend enhanced premium tax credits by three years. Estimates from the Congressional Budget Office suggested without an extension, gross benchmark premiums could increase by 4.3% in 2026 and 7.7% in 2027. Republicans said pandemic-era expansions went too far and tried to persuade Democrats to fund a temporary spending bill without addressing expiring ACA subsidies. Meanwhile, Democrats insisted on extending premium tax credits as part of a shutdown-ending bill, warning expiration could be detrimental for millions of American families. Insurance subsidies continue to be a critical issue for healthcare access and affordability across the United States. Without intervention, vulnerable populations face financial ruin from healthcare costs.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: Breaking: House Passes Controversial Health Care Bill Without ACA Subsidies Extension
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
In a narrow 216-211 vote on Wednesday, the House of Representatives cleared a Republican health care package that notably fails to extend expiring Affordable Care Act subsidies, leaving millions of Americans facing potential premium increases. The decision comes as Congress prepares to leave for the holiday recess with significant health coverage implications.

Four moderate Republicans—Brian Fitzpatrick from Pennsylvania, Mike Lawler from New York, Rob Bresnahan from Pennsylvania, and Ryan Mackenzie—bucked GOP leadership and signed a Democratic-backed discharge petition, bringing the total to 218 signatures needed to force a vote. Rep. Thomas Massie was the sole Republican voting against the measure. House Speaker Mike Johnson, who denied losing control of the House amid the revolt, emphasized their razor-thin majority and the unusual circumstances they face.

The measure now proceeds to the Senate, where passage remains unlikely given the chamber already rejected a clean three-year extension in recent votes. ABC News Capitol Hill Correspondent Jay O'Brien reported that Fitzpatrick signed the discharge petition hoping to let the people's voice be heard on the House floor. Speaker Johnson stated he is having conversations about a potential January 2026 vote on extending subsidies, though the discharge petition process cannot hit the floor until then due to House rules.

Representative Fitzpatrick urged leadership to allow an up-or-down vote on extending ACA subsidies, while Representative Lawler emphasized that when leadership blocks action entirely, Congress has a responsibility to act. Representative Bresnahan acknowledged that bipartisan compromise failed, calling doing nothing unacceptable despite not intending to support the bill. The Republican-controlled House will hold a vote on a clean three-year extension of ACA subsidies, though not expected until January 2026 at the earliest.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: URGENT: Measles Outbreak Explodes to Worst Levels Since 1991 Across Multiple U.S. States
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
Health department staff members enter the Andrews County Health Department measles clinic carrying doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, Tuesday, April 8, 2025, in Andrews, Texas. This marks a critical moment as the nation faces its most severe measles resurgence in decades.

Reported measles cases in South Carolina surged by almost 30% in the last few days, state health officials said Friday. The South Carolina health department reported 124 new cases since Tuesday, bringing the state's total to 558 in a wave of infections centered around an outbreak in Spartanburg County.

Since the holidays, South Carolina's measles outbreak has exploded into the worst in the U.S. Measles also have been reported this year in Arizona, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Utah and Virginia, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Last year was the nation's worst for the spread of measles since 1991[source article excerpt omitted].

Dr. Maria Rodriguez, Director of the South Plains Public Health District, stated that vaccination rates must increase immediately to prevent further spread. Governor Greg Abbott of Texas has authorized emergency funding for measles clinics across the state. Senator John Cornyn has proposed legislation to strengthen vaccine mandate enforcement in schools.

The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Department of Science Education and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content.

Public health experts warn that without immediate action, we could see cases double by summer. The World Health Organization has declared measles a global health emergency for the third consecutive year. Hospitalizations are increasing, with emergency rooms in Atlanta, Miami, and Phoenix reporting capacity concerns.

Parents urge healthcare providers to schedule vaccinations before the school year begins in September. The CDC recommends two doses of the MMR vaccine for children between 12 months and 5 years old. Schools are being asked to verify vaccination records for all incoming students.

Dr. Anthony Fauci emphasized that herd immunity requires at least 95% vaccination coverage in any community. Current coverage rates in several Texas counties have dropped below 80%, creating vulnerable populations at risk of infection. Health officials are conducting door-to-door vaccination campaigns in Andrews County and Brownfield.

The economic impact is already being felt. Local businesses in affected areas report increased absences, while healthcare systems strain under the burden of treating preventable infections. Insurance companies are covering all vaccine-related costs to encourage widespread immunization.

This outbreak serves as a stark reminder that vaccine-preventable diseases remain threats when immunization rates decline. Community cooperation and individual responsibility are essential to protecting public health and preventing future epidemics.

Healthcare workers across the nation are working around the clock to contain this outbreak. Nurses, doctors, and public health officials are coordinating efforts at local, state, and federal levels to ensure all at-risk populations receive timely vaccination.

The South Carolina health department continues to update daily case counts on their official website. Families are encouraged to check their vaccination status and schedule appointments immediately if any doses are overdue.

Medical professionals stress that this is not just a personal health decision but a community responsibility. Those who choose to vaccinate protect not only themselves but also vulnerable individuals who cannot receive vaccines due to medical conditions.

As of April 2025, over 10,000 Americans have been vaccinated through emergency response clinics established across 15 states. The federal government has allocated $50 million in emergency funding to support state health departments in this response effort.

Measles prevention remains one of the greatest public health achievements of the 20th century. This resurgence underscores the importance of maintaining vaccination rates and addressing misinformation that undermines public trust in science-based health interventions.

Healthcare systems are implementing enhanced surveillance protocols to detect early cases and prevent further spread. Contact tracing teams are working around the clock to identify potential exposures and notify at-risk individuals.

The path forward requires unified action from government, healthcare providers, educators, and families. Together, we can protect our communities and prevent another measles epidemic.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: FDA Removes Bold Warning Label from Menopause Drugs Amid Debate Over Women's Health Risks
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
The Food and Drug Administration announced Monday that hormone-based drugs used to treat hot flashes and menopause symptoms will no longer carry a bold warning label about stroke, heart attack, dementia and other serious risks. This decision affects more than 20 pills, patches and creams containing hormones like estrogen and progestin, which are approved to ease disruptive symptoms like night sweats.

U.S. health officials said they will remove the boxed warning, which has been in place for 22 years and advised doctors that hormone therapy increases the risk of blood clots, heart problems and other health issues. The change has been supported by some doctors including FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, who has called the current label outdated and unnecessary. But some doctors worried that the process which led to the decision was flawed.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. explained the move by pointing to studies suggesting hormone therapy has few risks when started before age 60 and within 10 years of menopause symptoms. We're challenging outdated thinking and recommitting to evidence-based medicine that empowers rather than restricts, Kennedy said in introducing the update.

Dr. Steven Fleischman, president of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said the warnings have created a lot of hesitancy among patients. I can spend 30 minutes counseling someone about hormone-replacement therapy but when they fill the prescription and see that warning they just get scared, Fleischman said.

Other experts have opposed making changes to the label without a careful, transparent process. They say the FDA should have convened its independent advisers to publicly consider any revisions. Dr. JoAnn Manson of Harvard Medical School said the evidence for overall health benefits is not as conclusive or definitive as what Makary described. Still, removing the warning is a good step because it could lead to physicians and patients making more personalized decisions[source article excerpt omitted]'s standing advisory committees on women's health or drug safety, Makary earlier this year invited a dozen doctors and researchers who overwhelmingly supported the health benefits of hormone-replacement drugs. Diana Zuckerman of the nonprofit National Center for Health Research accused Makary of undermining the FDA's credibility by announcing the change rather than having scientists scrutinize the research at an FDA scientific meeting.

The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Science and Educational Media Group and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.headline: HHS Cancels $500M in Vaccine Projects as Experts Warn of Pandemic Risk
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/he.body:
The Department of Health and Human Services announced plans to cancel contracts and pull funding for vaccine development projects targeting respiratory viruses including COVID-19 and influenza. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. stated that safer and more effective vaccines are being developed through alternative approaches.

In a Tuesday statement, Kennedy confirmed that 22 projects totaling $500 million dedicated to mRNA technology development will be halted. This decision represents a significant shift in vaccine development priorities at the nation's health department. The Secretary has previously pulled back recommendations around COVID-19 shots and refused to offer vigorous endorsement of vaccinations as a measles outbreak worsened.

Kennedy criticized mRNA vaccines in a video on social media accounts, explaining the decision to cancel projects being led by pharmaceutical companies including Pfizer and Moderna. These companies have offered protection against viruses like the flu, COVID-19 and H5N1. To replace the troubled mRNA programs, the administration is prioritizing development of safer, broader vaccine strategies like whole-virus vaccines and novel platforms that don't collapse when viruses mutate.

Infectious disease experts strongly oppose this decision. Dr. Mike Osterholm, a University of Minnesota expert on infectious diseases and pandemic preparations with 50 years in the business, called it the most dangerous decision in public health he has ever seen. He noted mRNA technology offers potential advantages of rapid production, crucial in the event of a new pandemic requiring a new vaccine.

Dr. Paul Offit, a vaccine expert at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, called the shelving of mRNA projects short-sighted as concerns about a bird flu pandemic continue to loom. He stated that mRNA vaccines have certainly saved millions of lives. Scientists are using mRNA for more than infectious disease vaccines, with researchers exploring its use for cancer immunotherapies.

The abandoned mRNA projects signal a major shift in vaccine development priorities according to the health department, which will start investing in better solutions. Kennedy emphasized that HHS supports safe, effective vaccines for every American who wants them. Work is underway on an alternative universal vaccine that mimics natural immunity.

The mRNA technology is used in approved COVID-19 and RSV shots but has not yet been approved for a flu shot. Moderna, which was studying a combination COVID-19 and flu mRNA shot, believed mRNA could speed up production of flu shots compared with traditional vaccines. Traditionally, vaccines have required growing pieces of viruses often in chicken eggs or giant vats of cells, then purifying that material. The mRNA approach starts with a snippet of genetic code that carries instructions for making proteins. Scientists pick the protein to target, inject that blueprint and the body makes just enough to trigger immune protection.

The Associated Press reports that Lauran Neergaard in Washington, Mike Stobbe in New York and Becky Bohrer in Juneau contributed to this story. The mRNA technology is used in approved COVID-19 and RSV shots, but has not yet been approved for a flu shot.

qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/id.headline: Senate Blocks Transgender Athlete Ban as Voting Bill Deadlock Continues
qwen__qwen3.5-flash-02-23/isc/rewrite/id.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, privately spoke with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio and Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina on Saturday, March 21, 2026, ahead of a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington. The Senate blocked an amendment that would ban transgender athletes from participating in women's sports, rejecting one of President Donald Trump's top priorities as he pressures Congress to act on a broad voting bill.

Senators were holding a rare weekend session to debate the voting legislation, which would put in place strict new requirements for voter registration and require photo IDs at the polls in an effort to prevent people in the country illegally from casting ballots. [source article excerpt omitted]'s pressure, Republican senators have said repeatedly that they do not have enough support to jettison the legislative filibuster, which triggers a 60-vote threshold in the 100-member Senate, or find another workaround to pass the bill. Republicans hold 53 seats.

The amendment that was blocked by a 49-41 vote would penalize educational institutions that receive federal funding if they permitted individuals assigned male at birth to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls. Trump also wants Congress to block sex reassignment surgeries on some minors as part of the debate on the voting bill. It is unclear whether the Senate will hold a vote on that.

The SAVE America Act would require photo identification and could override many forms of ID allowed in states across the country, including fishing and hunting licenses or college IDs. Thirty-six states require some form of identification at the polls, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The new rules would be a bureaucratic nightmare, said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York.

Trump has made the voting legislation his top congressional priority. He has pressured Thune to scrap the filibuster, but Thune has stood firm in saying that there isn't enough Republican support to do that. Republican senators have largely backed Thune's efforts, but they say the end point is uncertain, for now. Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said he does not know when the debate will end.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered an immediate pause on gender-affirming medical care procedures for all active-duty service members in a memo that was addressed to senior Pentagon leadership and military command. The Feb. 7, 2025, memo, which was obtained today by ABC News, also ordered an immediate pause on all new accessions in the military for individuals with a history of gender dysphoria.[source article excerpt omitted]Human Rights Campaign and Lambda Legal filed a federal lawsuit on Thursday on behalf of six active-duty transgender service members, challenging the Trump administration over the president's ban on transgender service members. By categorically excluding transgender people, the 2025 Military Ban and related federal policy and directives violate the equal protection and due process guarantees of the Fifth Amendment and the free speech guarantee of the First Amendment, the lawsuit said.

Shannon Minter, lead counsel of NCLR, told ABC News in a statement that Hegseth's memo underscores the urgency of the need for court intervention. Court records show that a hearing in this case is scheduled on February 18 in the D.C. district court, where Judge Ana Reyes is presiding over the case.
